A parameter-sparse state-space framework for characterizing coastal dune-aquifer architecture from manual dipwell records

M. Hollingham

Draft --- 2026

# Abstract

**Study region:** Newborough Warren, Anglesey, Wales. This is a coastal dune aquifer on the Irish Sea, monitored by 88 manual dipwells over 21 years and one climate station.

**Study focus:** Dune-slack vegetation depends on water-table depth within a band a few tens of centimetres wide. Distributed flow models of dune sand, however, need conductivity and thickness fields that are costly and poorly constrained. We ask whether routine dipwell records alone can resolve dune-aquifer architecture. We couple hierarchical clustering of hydrograph dynamics to a three-term state-space model, with terms for recharge, atmospheric draw and head-dependent drainage towards a level the fit itself sets. The model is fitted at each well from monthly rainfall and temperature, without coring, hydraulic testing or flow-model calibration.

**New hydrological insights for the region:** The data resolve five hydrogeological clusters, each with distinct mechanistic coefficients. Once corrected for canopy interception, apparent storage coefficients converge across them; the coastal forest cluster sits just above the open-dune range. The contrasts in behaviour are therefore consistent with control by the surface and land cover rather than by storage. The fit closes the mean water balance to within 1.7% of losses. Heads alone do not identify how the loss splits between drainage and evapotranspiration: drainage takes 45% at the median well under the adopted model, and 31--55% under an independent water balance. Against a linear benchmark, the model raises median iterative Nash--Sutcliffe efficiency from 0.38 to 0.83.

**Keywords:** coastal dune aquifer; dune slack; state-space model; apparent storage coefficient; groundwater characterization

Highlights

-   Dune-aquifer architecture resolved from manual dipwells and one climate station
-   Water balance closes; its drainage--evaporation split is bounded, not identified
-   Iterative forecast skill rises from NSE 0.38 to 0.83 over a linear benchmark
-   Interception-corrected apparent storage is broadly uniform across clusters

# 1. Introduction

[]{#introduction}Coastal dune slacks are among the most hydrologically sensitive habitats in north-west Europe. They are defined by a water table that fluctuates seasonally within a narrow envelope. The wet- and dry-slack vegetation communities of conservation interest occupy a band of summer-minimum depth only a few tens of centimetres wide (Davy et al., 2006; Curreli et al., 2013). Groundwater, not surface management, sets that envelope. Understanding the conservation status of a dune system therefore needs a quantitative account of how its aquifer fills, stores and releases water: how recharge reaches the water table, how evaporative demand and lateral drainage remove it, and how these processes vary across the site\'s geomorphological range.

Conventional hydrogeological methods struggle to characterize that architecture in dunes. Distributed groundwater models of the MODFLOW family need hydraulic conductivity fields, aquifer-thickness surfaces and boundary fluxes, which are expensive to measure and poorly constrained in unconsolidated, rapidly transmissive dune sand. An earlier distributed model of Newborough Warren met exactly these calibration difficulties (Betson et al., 2002). Slug and pumping tests sample only the ground immediately around a borehole, and interpolating a parameter field across several square kilometres of dunes needs dense borehole networks that are rarely available.

Yet many dune sites are monitored, often for decades, with low-cost instruments that distributed models cannot use directly: manual dipwells read monthly, and a nearby meteorological station. This paper asks a methodological question. Can that routine record, on its own, resolve the hydrogeological architecture of a dune aquifer --- its storage, recharge sensitivity and drainage behaviour? And can it do so in enough spatial detail to support conservation interpretation, without coring, hydraulic testing or calibrated continuous-flow modelling?

We develop and demonstrate such a framework. At its core is a three-term state-space model (SSM) fitted separately at each well. It splits the monthly change in water-table position into three terms: recharge, proportional to rainfall; atmospheric draw, proportional to potential evapotranspiration; and head-dependent drainage, proportional to the height of the water table above a base level fitted with the other coefficients. It is the exponential-response model of transfer-function practice, written month by month. A companion methods paper (Hollingham, 2026c) sets out the model and tests how far its forecasts can be trusted, on recent years held back from the fit and on two older records. Here the model is a characterization tool. Each of its three fitted coefficients can be interpreted: recharge sensitivity, atmospheric draw, and the rate at which the water table returns to its own mean. The only forcing they need is monthly rainfall and temperature from a single station.

Around this core we build several independent characterizations that check one another. First, before any model is fitted, hierarchical clustering of hydrograph *dynamics* divides the network into spatially coherent hydrogeological units. Its correlation-based distance separates temporal behaviour from absolute water-table elevation. The mechanistic coefficients must then reproduce this structure independently. A pattern-matching affinity analysis extends the classification to wells with shorter records and picks out the gradational transition zones between units.

Next, the SSM is benchmarked against a traditional linear model under iterative simulation. Where it gains most then becomes a non-invasive diagnostic of where head-dependent drainage governs the aquifer. A water-balance decomposition, built directly from the fitted coefficients, quantifies recharge and loss at each cluster under identical climate forcing. An independent water-table-fluctuation estimate of the apparent storage coefficient, Sₐ (the "apparent specific yield" of Healy and Cook, 2002), tests whether the contrasts in behaviour between units reflect real differences in subsurface storage or boundary conditions at the surface. Finally, interpolating the per-well coefficients gives continuous maps of recharge sensitivity, atmospheric draw and drainage rate. It also gives a mean head surface with its flow field and, at each well, a water-balance residual that shows where the three-term model closes.

Long-term trends near the coast also carry an external forcing. Where a shoreline is eroding, the seaward drainage boundary migrates landward and deepens the nearby water table independently of climate. That forcing is the subject of a companion paper (Hollingham, 2026f) and is not treated here.

We demonstrate the framework at Newborough Warren, a coastal dune system on Anglesey, north-west Wales. The site has been monitored for twenty-one years by eighty-eight dipwells (eighty-nine monitoring points, including the Llyn Rhos-Ddu lake gauge). They span its full geomorphological range, from lake-margin and open-dune slacks to a mature coniferous plantation on the elevated landward flank. The density and length of the record make it an unusually good proving ground. It is large enough to test whether the framework recovers structure that is independently visible in the raw hydrographs, and varied enough to span the contrast between a shallow, fast-cycling open dune and a slower-draining forested interior.

The objectives of this paper are therefore: (i) to apply the state-space model of Hollingham (2026c) as a characterization framework; (ii) to demonstrate that hydrograph-dynamics clustering, mechanistic SSM coefficients, model-benchmarking diagnostics, water-balance decomposition and apparent-storage estimation converge on a single, internally consistent picture of aquifer architecture; (iii) to map that architecture continuously across the site and identify where the three-term water balance closes and where it does not; and (iv) to assess the framework's transferability to other dune systems monitored by routine dipwell networks.

Two management interventions took place at the site: dune scraping and a partial clearfell of the plantation. A companion paper quantifies their hydrological effects in a before-after-control-impact design (Hollingham, 2026b). They are not treated here; the plantation enters only as a land-cover boundary condition. The intervention dates --- the December 2017 clearfell and the dune-scrape years --- are the author's recollection from monitoring the site. The April 2015 CEH36 scrape is separately documented. No documentary record of the operations has been obtained.

# []{#anchor}2. Study site

Newborough Warren occupies the south-western tip of the Isle of Anglesey in north-west Wales (Figure 1). The modern dune system is a late-Holocene feature. The present dunes developed over previously cleared agricultural land following storms in 1330 (Ranwell, 1958; Rhind et al., 2001). The site has no perennial surface drainage. Flow lines shown on later figures are DEM-derived flow-accumulation paths, included for spatial reference.

Weakly permeable glacial till underlies the dune field and forms the effective base of the sand aquifer. A bedrock ridge, demarked by the 20 m AOD contour, trends south-south-west to north-north-east. It forms the northern boundary of the study area and outcrops within the northern plantation. The hydrological study area is defined by the extent of the DEM-derived flow network and covers approximately 865 ha. The dipwell network spans a core zone of roughly 720 ha within it, lying entirely on the south-eastern flank of the ridge. Dune terrain on the north-western flank drains toward the Malltraeth estuary. It is hydrologically separate and is not considered here.

The substrate divides the aquifer south-east of the ridge into two contrasting blocks (Stratford et al., 2007). In the east, shallow sand over till and estuarine deposits constrains storage and produces a responsive, flashy water-table regime. In the west, deep aeolian sand has built up over a broader platform, allowing substantial groundwater storage and strongly buffered seasonal fluctuations. The present data do not resolve the cause of this east--west contrast (Section 5.1). It may reflect two distinct substrate bodies, or a single estuarine-clay base that crops out on the higher eastern and southern ground and dips beneath the surface toward Caernarfon Bay, thinning the sand column in the east and thickening it toward the south-west.

The aquifer discharges principally across the south-western foreshore of Caernarfon Bay and the southern and eastern coast of the Menai Strait. Llyn Rhos-Ddu, a small lake within the warren, acts as a near-fixed-head body. It is the dominant local drainage sink for the immediately adjacent wells. It receives groundwater throughout the year, because the regional water table maintains its head above the lake surface (Stratford et al., 2007).

The north of the study area is managed plantation, mostly mature Corsican pine. It enters this analysis only as a land-cover boundary condition: its canopy intercepts part of the rainfall before it reaches the ground, and this interception is treated below as a reduction in the surface input to the forested clusters, not as a management variable. The dune-slack communities of the open system are classified under the National Vegetation Classification as SD15b (wet slack) and SD16 (dry slack). Their community-mean water-table levels (Curreli et al., 2013) give the ecological reference frame for the site but are not used analytically in this paper.

# 3. Data and methods

## 3.1 Groundwater and climate records

[]{#groundwater-and-climate-records}The main dataset is a network of manually read dipwells. Water-table elevation is read roughly monthly, at the end of each month, and represents the level for the month just ended. By field convention, a reading on or before the fifteenth is assigned to the previous month and a later reading to the same month. Every monthly series is therefore indexed by the month the reading belongs to, not the day it was taken. Wells with long enough records form the reference network used for model fitting. The remaining wells, with shorter records, form an extended network classified by pattern matching (Section 3.3). Water levels are expressed in metres above ordnance datum and, for the state-space model, as depth below the ground surface at each well.

Climate forcing comes from the Royal Air Force Valley station. Monthly precipitation totals are used directly. Potential evapotranspiration (PET) is computed by the Thornthwaite method from monthly mean temperature and station latitude, with the heat index summed over the trailing twelve months rather than the calendar year so that it is defined for a record that does not end in December. Thornthwaite PET is an empirical index of atmospheric evaporative demand. Unlike Penman--Monteith, it defines no specific reference surface, which affects how the atmospheric-draw coefficient is read (Section 5.3). Rainfall and PET are totals for the same calendar month as the water-table change they are paired with. Consistent with the end-of-month readings, no rainfall lag is applied.

## 3.2 Hierarchical clustering of hydrograph dynamics

[]{#anchor}Agglomerative hierarchical clustering with Ward's minimum-variance linkage (Ward, 1963) divides the reference network into hydrogeologically distinct zones. The distance is the Pearson correlation distance between standardized well hydrographs. It compares the *shape* of seasonal and inter-annual water-table change and discards absolute elevation, so two wells that rise and fall together count as similar whatever their mean depth. The clustering therefore separates the dynamic hydrogeological signature --- the timing and relative amplitude of filling and draining --- from the topographic offset between wells.

The number of clusters is selected by a dual-metric approach that combines two measures. The first is the Ward's merge-distance profile, which identifies the partition at which further agglomeration incurs a disproportionate increase in within-cluster variance. The second is the mean silhouette coefficient (Rousseeuw, 1987), computed on the same correlation distance, which favours partitions with well-separated, internally coherent groups.

Each cluster is then described by its seasonal amplitude: the range between the 10th and 90th percentiles of each well's monthly water level, with the median taken over the cluster's wells (Figure 6). Amplitude plays no part in forming the clusters or in choosing their number: the correlation distance discards it.

## 3.3 Network extension by Pearson affinity analysis

[]{#anchor-1}Pearson affinity analysis extends the classification from the reference network to the wells with shorter records. Unlike the mechanistic models, it works on the raw observed series, with no model fitted. Each well's hydrograph is correlated with every cluster centroid, and the well joins the cluster it correlates with most strongly. The correlation delta between that cluster and the next-strongest sorts membership into tiers: core members, with one clear dominant affinity, and wells whose affinities to neighbouring clusters are close. A multi-cluster affinity flag marks wells that several centroids match almost equally well. Where these flags concentrate, they mark the gradational transition zones, in which the boundaries between units are diffuse rather than sharp. The extended-network wells are classified for spatial completeness and are not used in the cluster-level mechanistic fits.

We also tested whether a well's cluster-mates can fill the months it was not read. Where two wells were both read, a straight line relating one to the other is fitted. That line then turns the donor's reading in a missing month into an estimate for the target.

To test this, we hid months that had been read and checked how well each method put them back. We did this twice, for two stretches of 54 months: one starting in March 2006, near the start of the record, and one ending with its last month. Every well read in at least 80 % of a stretch was a target. Its hidden months were filled in five ways: from the nearest well that correlates with it at r ≥ 0.95; from the best-correlated well; from the nearest well in the same cluster that meets the same threshold; from the median of its cluster; and from the SSM run on climate alone. To keep the test fair, each line was fitted only on months outside the hidden stretch (at least 48), the clusters were worked out again without the hidden months, and donors within 50 m of their target were left out as near-twins. Each method was scored by how far it missed the mean spring (March--May) water level of each hidden year. The method to use was chosen by a rule set before the test: the smallest median miss over both stretches.

We also asked whether the clusters held in the past. The Countryside Council for Wales (CCW) read some of today's wells from 1989 to 1996. We grouped those wells on their 1989--96 readings alone, by the method of Section 3.2, and compared the groups with today's clusters. Agreement was scored by the adjusted Rand index (0 for chance, 1 for identical) and checked against random groupings. By a rule set before the test, the clusters count as having held only if agreement beats chance (p \< 0.05) and at least two-thirds of the pairs of wells that share a cluster today were grouped together then. As a check on the method, the same wells were also grouped on their modern readings.

## 3.4 State-space model and the displacement formulation

[]{#anchor-2}The mechanistic core of the framework is the monthly linear-reservoir model of Hollingham (2026c), in the form that paper calls the fitted-floor model: the level to which drainage returns is fitted with the other coefficients rather than fixed at a surveyed datum. It relates the monthly change in water-table position to climate forcing and to the antecedent head. For a given well or cluster centroid, the model is

> Δh(t) = α_B + β₁·P(t) − β₂·PET(t) − β₃·h_disp(t−1)

where Δh(t) is the change in water-table position during month t, and P(t) and PET(t) are the month-t precipitation and potential-evapotranspiration totals. The three β coefficients are reported as positive quantities. β₁ (recharge sensitivity) is the water-table rise per unit rainfall. β₂ (atmospheric draw) is the decline per unit PET. β₃ (proportional drainage decay) is the fraction of a departure from the water table\'s own equilibrium level that drainage removes each month. α_B is the fitted intercept.

The drainage term is driven by the displacement above the datum at the start of the month, so the level at the start of a month sets that month's drainage. Using the level at its end, h(t), would regress the change on its own end-point:

> h_disp(t−1) = z₀ + h(t−1)

where h is the water-table position (negative below ground) and z₀ is a fixed reference level, 3.7 m below the ground surface. The model is fitted by ordinary least squares with an intercept. Because α_B absorbs any reference level, z₀ drops out of the fit: the level at which the fitted drainage is zero, z_B = z₀ − α_B/β₃, is fitted rather than assumed, and it lies near each well\'s own mean. A departure from that level shrinks by a factor (1 − β₃) each month, so its e-folding time, −1/ln(1 − β₃), is a mean-reversion time and a property of the record rather than a recession towards a physical floor. β₃ is bounded to keep drainage positive; the record does not identify it everywhere. Hollingham (2026c, Sections 2.2 and 5.3) derives the model as a monthly step of the standard exponential-response model and sets out what the fitted base is and is not. The same paper tests, and does not adopt, a fixed drainage floor at 3.7 m and at mean high water (Section 7 there).

The lumped catchment storage coefficient, LCSC = 100/β₁, summarizes the recharge sensitivity of each unit: it is the depth of rainfall needed to raise the water table by 100 mm, so a lower LCSC means greater recharge sensitivity. LCSC/100 = 1/β₁ is itself an apparent storage coefficient: the rain needed per unit rise, as the water-table-fluctuation Sₐ is the recharge per unit rise (Section 3.8). The fitted coefficients fold together vegetation effects, storage and soil-moisture dynamics. For this reason, in an open-boundary system like this one the recharge term can absorb unmeasured boundary fluxes into β₁ (Young, 2011; Knotters and van Walsum, 1997). The residual analysis (Section 3.9) and the Sₐ estimation (Section 3.8) address this.

A depth-dependent extension was evaluated at cluster level as a diagnostic of depth coupling (Section 5.2). In it, β₂ is replaced by β₂·exp(−d_w/L_E), so that atmospheric draw declines as the water-table depth d_w increases, and L_E is found by grid search, as its reciprocal 1/L_E. The fixed-β₂ model is used throughout, as an effective depth-averaged parameterization.

The model is fitted at two scales, each on a stated record. The mechanistic characterization (Table 1) is fitted to each cluster-mean hydrograph over its full record. Averaging suppresses single-well noise and gives one coefficient set per zone, so a cluster coefficient is a centroid, not a property of every member, and it depends on the partition. The per-well coefficients are fitted on the same 98 calendar months at every well, January 2018 to February 2026, so that wells are compared under the same climate. A month in which a well was dry stays in the window as a level at or below the deepest the dipwell can read, not as a gap. These coefficients give the ranges (Table 5), the surfaces (Figures 11--13) and the benchmark (Section 3.5). The per-well drainage timescales (Figure 14) are instead fitted on each well\'s full record, because 98 months do not resolve the slow forest recession. Hollingham (2026c, Section 4.3) reports, cluster by cluster, how much record the drainage coefficient needs before it stabilizes.

## 3.5 Model benchmarking against a traditional linear model

[]{#anchor-3}The predictive value of the head-dependent drainage term is tested against a traditional linear model (TLM): the same model without the drainage term and with a free intercept. The TLM is fitted at every reference well on the 98-month comparison window and run freely over the same months from the first observed level, so the test is in-sample. Hollingham (2026c) sets out the models, the protocol and the network results, for both the fixed-floor and the fitted-floor forms; the benchmark here uses the fitted-floor SSM. It tests the drainage term against its absence; it does not choose between the two forms, which the same paper compares out of sample. Here, the per-well gain in iterative Nash--Sutcliffe efficiency of the SSM over the TLM is mapped across the network (Figure 10). The map shows where the drainage term is indispensable to prediction and where the aquifer approximates a linear climate response.

## 3.6 Spatial coefficient mapping and within-forest regression

[]{#anchor-4}The per-well SSM coefficients are interpolated piecewise-linearly, on a Delaunay triangulation of the wells, over a regular grid on a LiDAR-derived digital elevation model, with ridge cells and non-aquifer areas masked. This gives continuous surfaces of recharge sensitivity, atmospheric draw and drainage rate, and a surface of model-fit quality. The surfaces show aquifer behaviour in space, complementing the cluster-level summaries.

Within the forested zone the per-well coefficients span much of the site-wide range. There, they are regressed against elevation, distance from the ridge and easting, and against canopy density measured at each well from the aerial imagery (Section 4.8). The regression asks whether the within-forest variation follows topographic position and water-table depth, or differences in canopy. Because the subsurface beneath the plantation is not cored, elevation and position stand in for substrate, and the regression isolates this topographic control on the mechanistic coefficients beneath a single land cover.

## 3.7 Mean monthly water-balance decomposition

[]{#mean-monthly-water-balance-decomposition}The fitted cluster coefficients split the mean monthly water balance of each cluster into its component fluxes under identical climate forcing. Recharge is β₁ times mean monthly precipitation; atmospheric draw is β₂ times mean monthly PET; drainage is β₃ times the mean height of the water table above the base level the model fits for each cluster (Section 3.4). All terms are in metres of water-table change per month, the natural unit of the state-space model, and are directly comparable between clusters that receive the same climate. The model is fitted on gross rainfall and above-canopy PET, so at the forested clusters the canopy's interception loss (24% of rainfall; Freeman, 2008, a single-plot, single-season measurement and the only site value) is already inside the evaporation term. It is shown as part of the evaporation and never added to the losses. The net monthly balance, recharge minus total losses, is the input an unmeasured boundary source would have to supply to maintain long-run equilibrium.

Alongside the head-space decomposition, an indicative volumetric conversion applies each cluster's head-space split to the full rainfall, so it needs no storage coefficient. Heads alone do not identify the split between evapotranspiration and drainage (Hollingham, 2026c). It is quoted from the SSM, beside the ratio of winter to summer recession rates. Two readings that need no fitted model are reported with them: the floor that the water balance puts under drainage, and the water-balance residual analysis of Hollingham (2026c) (Section 4.5).

## 3.8 Apparent storage coefficient by the water-table-fluctuation method

[]{#anchor-5}An independent estimate of storage, the apparent storage coefficient Sₐ, comes from the dipwell record by the water-table-fluctuation method (Healy and Cook, 2002). It is not the specific yield Sy of the sand: it lumps drainable porosity with the state of the capillary fringe and drainage within the month. Here Sₐ is the ratio of net recharge to the water-table rise it causes. The method is applied to the cluster-mean hydrographs. It keeps only months in which the water table rose and net recharge was positive, each above set thresholds, and it limits event-level estimates to a physically plausible range. Monthly data cannot isolate individual storm events, and at this resolution the method is known to conflate gravity drainage with capillary-fringe release. The estimates are therefore read as upper bounds on effective storage, not point estimates (Healy and Cook, 2002; Scanlon et al., 2002).

At the forested clusters, rainfall is corrected for canopy interception before net recharge is computed. Unlike the decomposition of Section 3.7, this method takes rainfall as recharge directly, so interception must be removed from it. The correction reduces only the rainfall input and leaves Thornthwaite PET unchanged. PET is an energy-based index of atmospheric demand, independent of land cover; reducing it for interception would conflate atmospheric demand with realized evapotranspiration and remove the same quantity from both sides of the balance. Comparing the corrected forest estimates with the open-dune range tests whether the attenuated water-table response beneath the canopy reflects the surface boundary condition or a genuinely different subsurface storage. The per-well event-median Sₐ values are also interpolated across the site, to see whether storage is uniform or steps at the cluster margins.

## []{#anchor-6}3.9 Spatial interpolation, flow field and water-balance residual

The mean water-table surface is built by ordinary kriging of each well's mean head with a spherical variogram. Kriging is generally preferred over deterministic interpolators, such as inverse-distance weighting, for mapping groundwater levels from sparse wells (Varouchakis and Hristopulos, 2013; Rao et al., 2022). It can take a drift on the ground surface (Desbarats et al., 2002), but here the drift was tested rather than assumed: three drifts were compared with ordinary kriging by leave-one-well-out error and by a physical test against Sentinel-2 wet-floor extents, and ordinary kriging was selected (Hollingham, 2026d, §3.8). The edges are anchored rather than extrapolated. Seaward, the anchor is the sea along the high-water mark, at a coastal head fitted to the coastal wells between mean tide level and mean high water (UKHO, 2026). Inland, the anchors are the Afon Braint, Llyn Rhos-Ddu and the ridge well CEH12. No elevation mask is applied. Flow arrows show the negative head gradient, one per 100 m square, sized by the gradient. No hydraulic conductivity or aquifer thickness enters them: they describe the flow geometry of the mapped surface, not the output of a calibrated continuous-flow model (Bear, 1972; Freeze and Cherry, 1979).

The water-balance residual measures, at each reference well, how well the three-term SSM closes the long-term water balance. It is the difference between modelled mean losses (atmospheric draw plus drainage) and modelled mean recharge, computed from the fitted coefficients. Gross rainfall is used at every well; interception is already in β₂·PET̄ (Section 3.7). A positive residual means modelled losses exceed modelled recharge, pointing to an inadequacy of the three-term model at that location or, in principle, to an unmodelled input. A near-zero residual means the three-term balance closes adequately. The residual is shown at the wells alone and is not interpolated: left out one well at a time, no interpolator predicts a withheld well's residual appreciably better than the network mean, so no surface is drawn. It is read as a structural diagnostic of where the model's three terms are sufficient, not as a quantified map of lateral inflow, because it also absorbs nonlinear soil-moisture storage dynamics, coefficient sensitivity and any systematic bias in the Thornthwaite PET estimate. Two independent analyses test the mechanistic attribution of the residual pattern: a cross-correlation lag analysis for distance-dependent transport from the ridge, and a seasonal climatology analysis for unmodelled summer evaporative demand.

## 3.10 Computational implementation

[]{#data-and-methods}[]{#computational-implementation}All pre-processing, statistical modelling and spatial mapping run as a numbered, sequential Python pipeline, using pandas and NumPy for time series and statsmodels for model fitting. Spatial interpolation and rendering use a LiDAR DEM. The state-space alignment and the drainage term are written once, in a shared model-utilities module that every SSM-fitting script calls, so all downstream analyses are consistent with the cluster-level fits. Running the published scripts in sequence reproduces the pipeline and its outputs.

# []{#anchor-7}4. Results

## []{#anchor-7}4.1 Climate and well-network characterization

The RAF Valley record shows that Newborough Warren has a persistent annual water surplus. Over the monitoring period, mean annual precipitation was approximately 891 mm and mean annual Thornthwaite PET approximately 652 mm, a P/PET ratio of about 1.36 (Figure 2). The surplus is strongly seasonal: winter rainfall exceeds evaporative demand by a wide margin, while in summer PET exceeds rainfall, so atmospheric demand on the aquifer falls mainly in the months of lowest recharge. Year-to-year variation in the water balance comes almost entirely from precipitation, not evaporative demand. Evaporative demand is strongly seasonal and has a small positive inter-annual trend (1.96 mm/yr over 2007--2025), but it varies by only about 3% about its mean, against about 19% for winter rainfall. The post-2013 summers have been warmer than the earlier baseline (Figure 3), which deepens the summer deficit.

The reference network comprises 66 wells with monthly water-table records over the 2005--2026 monitoring period. It is supplemented by 22 extended-network wells with shorter records, classified by pattern matching (Section 4.3). The median record length is well above a decade. This gives the spatial density needed to distinguish cluster-scale behaviour from site-wide climate forcing.

## []{#anchor-8}4.2 Network clustering and spatial architecture

Clustering the standardized hydrograph dynamics by Pearson correlation distance and Ward's linkage resolves five spatially coherent units under the dual-metric selection of k (Figure 4). They are a lake-margin unit (C1, Lake Edge), an open-dune unit (C2, Dune) and a western unit on deeper sand (C3, Western Residual), and two units beneath the Corsican pine plantation, distinguished by topographic position: C4, Main Forest, on the elevated ridge flank, and C5, Coastal Forest, on the lower coastal fringe (Figure 5). The clusters hold C1 = 7, C2 = 19, C3 = 26, C4 = 9 and C5 = 5 wells.

The five units recover the broad substrate contrast between the responsive, storage-limited east and the buffered, deeper-sand south-west (Stratford et al., 2007). The south-western unit (C3) is gradational toward both the open dune and the forest, rather than a sharply bounded block. The top Ward merge (linkage distance ≈0.99) separates C4 Main Forest from the other 57 wells. The east--west division, C1 and C2 against C3 and C5, follows at ≈0.61. C5 Coastal Forest therefore joins the western group rather than C4, despite sharing the pine canopy. Figure 6 shows the cluster-centroid hydrographs and seasonal amplitudes.

## 4.3 Affinity validation of the cluster structure

[]{#anchor-9}The Pearson affinity analysis supports the primary membership of 60 of the 66 reference wells. Membership tiers follow the correlation delta between the assigned cluster and the next-strongest one. A minority of wells are core members, with one clear dominant affinity; many others have closely competing affinities to neighbouring units. This is consistent with gradational rather than sharp boundaries in a contiguous, highly transmissive sand aquifer (Rao and Srinivas, 2006). Multi-cluster-affinity flags concentrate along the C1/C2/C3 transition and the forest--dune margin, marking the zones where geological and vegetative controls overlap.

The clusters also largely hold either side of the clearfell. Fitted on each half of the record alone, before and from January 2018, the two partitions of the 66 reference wells agree with each other far beyond chance (adjusted Rand index 0.58, p = 0.001), and each agrees with the full-record partition (0.65 before, 0.50 after). That is within the range two random halves of the record give (0.35--0.73). C4 Main Forest is identical in both halves, C1 Lake Edge loses one of its seven wells before 2018 and none after, and C2 Dune keeps at least 15 of its 19 wells in each. The division of the western sand is not stable: before 2018 the five C5 Coastal Forest wells group with C3 Western Residual, and from 2018 twelve of C3's 26 wells group with C5.

**Filling gaps from cluster-mates.** Copying from the nearest well in the same cluster did best, and was adopted. Over both 54-month test stretches it missed the hidden spring levels by a median 0.041 m, against 0.139 m for the SSM run on climate alone (Figure 7a). The early stretch (from March 2006, including the unexplained high water of 2006--08; Hollingham, 2026c) was harder for both: 0.065 against 0.149 m; the late stretch (to the end of the record) gave 0.037 against 0.132 m. The nearest well from any cluster (0.041 m) and the best-correlated well (0.043 m) did almost as well; the cluster median did worse (0.059 m). The further the donor, the larger the miss (Figure 7b; Spearman ρ = +0.61).

With that method, 69 wells gain 4,432 filled months, and 37 gaps have no suitable donor and stay empty. Filled months are marked as such and are not used anywhere else in this paper.

The clusters did not hold in 1989--96 by the rule (Figure 7c). Grouped on their early readings, the 12 CCW wells agree with today's clusters no better than chance (adjusted Rand index 0.03, p = 0.45), and only 28 % of the pairs that share a cluster today were grouped together then. Grouped on their modern readings, the same wells match today's clusters well (0.75), so the small number of wells is not the reason. The difference lies with three warren wells near the sea (NW6, NW5 and WMC2, now in C3). NW3 and NW4 (now C2) keep each other's company in both periods, as do NW11 and NW13 (C3); the three seaward wells moved with the first pair in 1989--96 and with the second today. Many early readings sit at the bottom of the pipe, below which the water table cannot be read. Keeping those readings raises the agreement to 0.20, and using only the 10 least-affected wells gives 0.17; neither passes the rule. The test therefore does not show that the clusters held, but with twelve wells over seven years it cannot show that they changed either.

## 4.4 Cluster mechanistic coefficients

The model, fitted to each cluster-centroid hydrograph, characterizes the five clusters mechanistically (Table 1). Every rate coefficient (β₁, β₂, β₃) is significant at p \< 0.001 at every cluster except the drainage coefficient at C4 Main Forest (p = 0.447), which the record does not identify.

Every coefficient shown is significant at p \< 0.001 except −β₃ at C4 Main Forest (p = 0.447).

  C1 Lake Edge          7         3.715   3.144   0.354   26.918     0.818
  C2 Dune               19        3.500   2.619   0.167   28.571     0.789
  C3 Western Residual   26        3.604   2.126   0.103   27.749     0.832

[]{#cluster-mechanistic-coefficients}Recharge sensitivity β₁ is highest at the Lake Edge (C1: 3.715), with the Western Residual (C3: 3.604) and the Dune (C2: 3.500) close behind, so a millimetre of rainfall raises the water table by a similar amount across the open dune. The two forested clusters have much lower recharge sensitivities (C4: 2.578, C5: 2.463), consistent with canopy interception reducing the rainfall that reaches the water table. As LCSC (100/β₁), 27--29 mm of rainfall raises the water table by 100 mm across the open dune, against 39--41 mm beneath the plantation: roughly 40% more rain for the same rise.

Atmospheric draw β₂ is highest at the Lake Edge (C1: 3.144), where the water table stands shallowest, and lowest at the Coastal Forest (C5: 1.335). The Dune (C2: 2.619) and the forest interior (C4: 2.499) follow, and the Western Residual (C3: 2.126) is lower than either. C5 carries the same pine canopy as C4 yet returns little more than half its atmospheric draw, so the canopy alone does not set the cluster-level contrast. Within the forest, β₂ follows elevation and water-table depth (Section 4.8), which points to topographic position rather than canopy as the dominant control.

The drainage decay −β₃ shows the strongest contrast of the three coefficients. It is highest at C1 (0.354), where rapid lateral exchange with Llyn Rhos-Ddu drives fast recovery. It falls through C2 (0.167) and C3 (0.103) to C5 (0.045). At C4 the centroid fit returns 0.010, but the record does not identify it, so the forest interior is reported as the cluster whose drainage the record cannot resolve rather than as the slowest (Hollingham, 2026c, Section 5.2).

## []{#anchor-10}4.5 Water balance and apparent storage

The head-space water-balance decomposition (Table 2; Figure 8a) closes to within 1.7% of total losses at every cluster, and within 0.6% outside C5. This closure is a property of the fit, not independent evidence: a model fitted to heads alone can be expected to close the mean balance (Hollingham, 2026c). It shows that the three terms are consistent with one another at the cluster mean without an unmeasured boundary term, not that each flux is confirmed. Recharge is highest at C1 (0.276 m/month) and lowest under the plantation (0.183--0.192 m/month), and total losses track recharge closely at every cluster.

How the loss divides between drainage and atmospheric draw is not identified from heads alone (Hollingham, 2026c). It is quoted here from the SSM, which gives every coefficient. Under the SSM, drainage takes 38% of the loss at C1, 45% at C2, 56% at C3 and 61% at C5. At C4 the SSM's drainage coefficient is not significant (p = 0.45), so its share there is not identified; Tables 2 and 3 give it by difference, marked †.

At C4, the SSM's β₃ is not significant (p = 0.45), so its drainage and split (†) are taken by difference, recharge less atmospheric draw, and are not estimates of β₃; its residual is therefore zero by construction and is not shown.

At the forested clusters canopy interception removes 214 mm/yr. Split by the SSM, drainage runs from 339 mm/yr at C1 to 544 mm/yr at C5; at C4 it is not identified. Evapotranspiration after interception runs from 133 mm/yr at C5 to 552 mm/yr at C1. A forest's total evaporative loss is I + ET: 346 mm/yr at C5, against 489 mm/yr at C2. The C5 figures are the least secure in the table. The record fixes C5's base level poorly (its intercept is not significant), its large drainage share follows from that, and a coastal forest that evaporates less than the open dune is therefore not a finding. **Figure 8.** Water-balance decomposition by cluster: (a) the mean monthly head-space balance under the SSM (recharge against atmospheric draw and drainage); (b) the indicative volumetric partition. In (b), the hatched band spans the ET/drainage split given by the SSM and by the ratio of winter to summer recession rates; it shows how far the split depends on the reading and is not a statistical confidence interval. Forest interception is part of the evaporation, not added to it (Section 3.7).

The WTF estimates of Sₐ (Table 4; Figure 9) test independently whether the cluster contrasts reflect storage architecture or surface boundary conditions. Uncorrected, the forested-cluster event-median Sₐ values sit above the top of the open-dune range (C4: 0.321, against an open-dune maximum of 0.312; C5: 0.364), because gross rainfall overstates the recharge flux beneath the canopy. Correcting the recharge term for canopy interception brings the cluster-level event medians down to 0.256 (C4) and 0.316 (C5). C4 then falls cleanly into the open-dune range (0.210--0.312), while C5 sits just above its upper edge. Taking instead the median of the per-well estimates gives 0.253 and 0.308; the two aggregations are reported separately throughout and are not interchangeable. The β₁ route gives the same reading independently. For the open-dune clusters, LCSC/100 (the lumped catchment storage coefficient of Section 3.4; Table 1) lies inside their WTF range, and at the forested clusters, scaled to throughfall, it falls in that range too.

The correction uses a single literature fraction rather than a fitted one, so the convergence is tested against that fraction directly. The forest clusters' event medians were re-evaluated over interception fractions from 0 to 0.40 (Section 3.8). Both fall within the open-dune range only for fractions between 0.28 and 0.32: C4 for every fraction up to 0.32, C5 only from 0.28. The C4 result therefore does not depend on the particular value 0.24, while C5 sits just outside the range at that value. For C4 this is reassuring: its convergence holds for every fraction up to 0.32, which includes the measured 0.24. C5 converges only if the canopy intercepts more than the measured quarter, so its convergence is not shown. The seasonal residual analysis of Section 5.4 is an independent check, and its cross-cluster ordering is likewise inconsistent with a mis-set fraction.

Across the three open-dune clusters, the per-well Sₐ values are well described by a planar spatial trend (n = 52, R² = 0.610, residual standard deviation 0.031). Sₐ rises by 0.070 per kilometre along an azimuth of 231°, so storage increases steadily toward the south-west. Both components are significant (easting −0.054 per kilometre, northing −0.044 per kilometre, each p \< 0.001). The trend is fitted to, and reported for, the open-dune network only. The forested wells lie outside its spatial domain, and the surface is not extrapolated beneath the plantation.

The C4 result indicates that the attenuated water-table response beneath the plantation reflects the surface canopy boundary condition rather than a fundamentally different substrate. The C5 estimate is the least reliable in the network: a majority of its rising-limb events imply an event-level Sₐ at or above the porosity of dune sand, so its median is constrained by the physical-plausibility limit rather than freely estimated, and it is reported only as a weak corroborator. All Sₐ medians are two to three times the literature specific yield of dune sand (0.08--0.12), the values assumed in Table 4. They are apparent storage, not a property of the sand, and are read as upper bounds (Healy and Cook, 2002; Scanlon et al., 2002).

## []{#anchor-11}4.6 Model benchmarking: SSM versus traditional linear model

Run freely over the comparison window, the SSM raises the median iterative Nash--Sutcliffe efficiency from 0.38 under the TLM to 0.83 across the 64 wells fitted on the window (Hollingham, 2026c, Section 4.1). Its efficiency is positive at all 64, against 53 for the TLM. The gain holds when the floor is fixed (Hollingham, 2026c, Section 7), but it is not uniform across the network (Figure 10). It is largest in the lake-proximal C1 Lake Edge, where head-dependent drainage is strongest (cluster median +1.02, against +0.51 at C2 and +0.31 at C3; e.g. CEH6: TLM −1.22 → SSM 0.89), and smallest under the forest (+0.26 at C4 and +0.28 at C5). At one well, in the coastal forest, the SSM scores below the TLM. The spatial pattern of the gain is therefore a non-invasive diagnostic of where head-dependent drainage governs the aquifer.

Two readings constrain the split without either form. The first is a floor. Actual evapotranspiration cannot exceed PET, and over 21 years the mean change in storage is negligible. Drainage is therefore at least the excess of rainfall over PET: 237--239 mm/yr in the open dune (C1--C3). The SSM's drainage there, 340--502 mm/yr (Table 3), lies above it, as does its 545 mm/yr at the coastal forest (C5).

The second is a water balance that takes storage from outside the fit (Hollingham, 2026c). Rainfall less PET gives a monthly surplus. The change in storage is the water-table change times the well's apparent storage coefficient, Sₐ, from the water-table-fluctuation method (Section 3.8), and whatever the surplus does not account for is taken as drainage. Over the 66 reference wells this puts drainage at 31% of the annual loss at the median well, against 45% under the SSM, and books more of the loss to the atmosphere: 0.74 to 0.97 of PET as actual evapotranspiration, cluster by cluster. The reading depends on Sₐ. When Sₐ is estimated from winter months instead, two regressions bracket it, of the water-table change on rainfall and of rainfall on the change (0.14--0.19 and 0.25--0.30 across the clusters), and the median share runs from 36% to 55%, a bracket that contains the SSM's 45%. The ratio of winter to summer recession rates, a share of summer recession rather than of the annual loss, gives 60, 35, 66, 51 and 73% at C1--C5. These are checks on the share, not revised drainage rates, and none of them replaces a measured flux.

![](Pictures/10000000000006400000048B7A7A5B76.jpg){width="16.164cm" height="13.0322cm"}**Figure 10.** Iterative Nash--Sutcliffe gain of the SSM over the traditional linear model at each reference well, interpolated across the network and masked over the dune ridges (colour scale capped at 1.5); the models and the free-running protocol are set out in Hollingham (2026c).

## []{#anchor-12}4.7 Spatial coefficient structure and drainage timescales

Interpolating the per-well coefficients gives continuous surfaces (per-well ranges in Table 5; Figures 11--13) whose broad structure follows the cluster boundaries while keeping substantial variation within clusters. Recharge sensitivity β₁ is highest in the north-east around the Lake Edge wells (per-well up to 4.93) and falls across the open dune to its lowest values beneath the forest. Atmospheric draw β₂ peaks in the C4 forest interior and along the northern dune beside the ridge, and is lowest in the Coastal Forest. Drainage rate β₃ has the strongest spatial contrast of any coefficient, from the fast-draining Lake Edge (per-well up to 0.415 per month) to the near-stagnant forest interior. There, one ridge-flank well (CEH14) returns a fitted base above the ground surface, where the model does not capture the boundary condition.

The drainage coefficient sets how fast a departure from a well\'s own level decays. Figure 14 maps the mean-reversion time 1/β₃ across the network: the number of months over which a departure decays to about a third of its size. The timescale is a property of the record, not a recession towards a physical floor, and the record returns the same timescale without any model at all (Hollingham, 2026c, Section 4.7). It is not a bound on amplitude: over a summer, drainage removes only a small part of a winter excess even where the timescale is short, and the much larger seasonal fall is set by evapotranspiration (the β₂ term).

The spatial pattern follows β₃ (Figure 13). The eastern open dune recovers fastest, the western dune is intermediate, and the forest interior is slowest of all. The drainage coefficient is not identified there, however, either at the centroid or at the wells ringed in Figure 14, so their times are not estimates. C5 Coastal Forest resembles the western dune despite sharing the pine canopy, which reinforces the substrate and elevation control. Hollingham (2026c, Table 3) tabulates mean-reversion times per cluster, with and without the model.

![](Pictures/100000010000075D0000061E2DE81B46.png){width="15.871cm" height="12.8435cm"}**Figure 14.** Mean-reversion time 1/β₃ (months, log scale) across the reference network, from each well\'s full-record fit under the SSM. C4 Main Forest wells are ringed: the SSM does not identify their drainage coefficient, so their times are not estimates. CEH13 (near-zero β₃) and CEH14 (drainage not defined) are excluded.

## 4.8 Substrate control within the forested zone

Within the forested zone the per-well coefficients span much of the site-wide range, and regression against elevation, distance from the ridge and easting identifies the underlying control (Table 6). Elevation dominates atmospheric draw β₂ (r = 0.964, p \< 0.001; R² = 0.929): wells higher on the ridge return systematically higher β₂. Drainage β₃ falls with elevation (r = −0.818, p \< 0.001). Both also vary with easting (β₂: r = 0.705, p = 0.005; β₃: r = −0.563, p = 0.037), though less strongly than with elevation. Distance from the ridge carries the same signal, correlating with both coefficients, but adds almost nothing to either regression once elevation is included (marginal R² gain 0.005 for β₂ and 0.001 for β₃), so elevation is the predictor these data support. Recharge β₁ has no significant relationship with elevation (p = 0.63), distance from the ridge (r = −0.435, p = 0.12) or easting (r = 0.479, p = 0.083).

β₂ does vary substantially across clusters (Table 1), but the cluster-level contrast is set by substrate, water-table depth and topographic position rather than by canopy maturation. The cleanest evidence is the C4--C5 split, a 2-fold difference in atmospheric draw within the plantation. C4 and C5 form two distinct groups rather than a continuum. They separate completely on β₂ --- C4 at 2.10--4.21, C5 at 1.03--1.82, with no overlap --- and on mean elevation (C4: 10.6 m, C5: 5.6 m; p = 0.0001). This matches the step from the elevated ridge flank, with its deeper water table and unsaturated zone, to the low coastal fringe, where the water table is shallower. The canopy is not uniform. Its density was measured at each forest well from the dated aerial imagery, as a canopy texture index (0 for the texture of open ground, 1 for that of mature conifer; values above 1 occur where understorey adds to the canopy\'s texture) in a 30 m disc around the well, on the frames before the 2017 felling. Across the fourteen wells the index ranges from 0.15 to 1.47, yet it is not significantly related to β₂ (r = 0.26, p = 0.37) or to elevation (r = 0.25, p = 0.39), while β₂ follows elevation (partial r = 0.989 given the canopy index). Holding elevation constant, canopy adds nothing (partial r = 0.09, p = 0.77), and the result is the same with 20 m and 50 m discs. C4 and C5 do not differ in canopy (medians 0.99 and 0.82). The C4--C5 separation therefore tracks elevation and water-table depth rather than canopy. The subsurface beneath the plantation is not cored; on the topographic and coefficient evidence the C4/C5 split is best read as a substrate-and-elevation discontinuity rather than an arbitrary division of a continuous canopy population.

## 4.9 Mean water-table surface and flow field

The water table is a single mound, highest beside the bedrock ridge (mean head 13.32 m AOD at CEH14). It falls to the coastal head along Caernarfon Bay and to the river and lake levels inland (Figure 15). Left out one at a time, the wells are predicted with a median absolute error of 0.14 m in the mean state and almost no bias (−0.005 m). Flow runs outward from the high point. It runs south and south-west to Caernarfon Bay across the west and centre, north towards Llyn Rhos-Ddu from the slacks beside the lake, and east and south-east to the Afon Braint. The pattern barely changes with the state of the aquifer. The median gradient is 0.0071 in the wet state and 0.0062 in the dry, and the median flow direction at the slacks turns 4.7° between the two.

## []{#anchor-13}4.10 Water-balance residual at the wells

The water-balance residual is modelled losses minus modelled recharge at each well, calculated from the fitted coefficients. It closes tightly and has a small systematic negative offset. Its magnitude carries no spatial structure, but its sign tilts east--west (Figure 16). Residuals span −0.0114 to +0.0206 m/month about a median of −0.0044 m/month. Of the 65 reference wells carrying a residual, 61 lie inside ±0.01 m/month and 49 are negative; CEH14 has no SSM residual (implied base above ground). The cluster medians are negative except at C5 Coastal Forest (+0.0028 m/month), from −0.0030 m/month at C1 Lake Edge to −0.0062 m/month at C2 Dune. Residual magnitude is uncorrelated with position on either axis (Spearman ρ = 0.09 against Easting, p = 0.49; ρ = −0.10 against Northing, p = 0.43). The signed residual falls eastward (ρ = −0.35 against Easting, p = 0.005) but not with Northing (ρ = −0.10, p = 0.45).

Residuals exceed +0.02 m/month at 1 well, NW3 (+0.0206) in C2 Dune, and 16 of the 65 are positive. The next largest are CEH4 (+0.0117) and NW6 (+0.0103), both in C3 Western Residual. All three lie in the open dune rather than at the ridge. No C4 Main Forest well is positive. The largest negative residuals fall at the lake-edge wells CEH25 (−0.0114 m/month) and CEH27 (−0.0095 m/month), both in C1 Lake Edge. Two independent diagnostic tests on the monthly SSM residual returned null results: a cross-correlation lag test for distance-dependent transport from the ridge, and a seasonal climatology test for unmodelled summer evaporative demand. No unmodelled flux is required to close the balance at any cluster.
